name: Teff

regionalSuitability.notes: Primary staple cereal of Ethiopian highlands. Thrives at 1800–2400m on black clay Vertisols.
Highland plateau cereal.

nitrogenEffect: Depletes — Teff is a heavy nitrogen consumer. Highly advised to precede or follow with nodulating legumes.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Shallow fibrous root system with exceptional waterlogging resilience on cracking clays.

description: Teff is Ethiopia and Eritrea's culturally foundational cereal grain. Gluten-free, iron-rich, and drought/waterlogging-hardy.

rotationCompatibility.notes: Preceding teff with faba bean significantly elevates grain protein and soil mineral nitrogen.

imageSource: FarmShield Botanical Archive & Wikimedia Commons (Eragrostis tef plant)
imageAttribution: A. Bekele / EIAR Research Extension & Wikimedia CC-BY-SA 3.0
imageLicense: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 / Fair Academic Use

name: Bread Wheat

regionalSuitability.notes: Highland wheat belt: Arsi, Bale, and West Shewa zones.
Rift Valley highland breadbasket.
Irrigated winter wheat along the Nile Valley.
Winter rainfall in Western Cape; dryland/irrigated in Free State.

nitrogenEffect: Depletes soil nitrogen reserves. Requires crop rotation with legumes or fertilizer replenishment.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Deeper than teff, moderate root density aiding subsoil porosity.

description: Essential caloric and commercial cereal across African temperate highlands and Mediterranean/irrigated basins.

rotationCompatibility.notes: Legume break crops break Fusarium and rust spores and restore organic nitrogen.

imageSource: Wikimedia Commons (Triticum aestivum mature wheat ears)

name: Maize

regionalSuitability.notes: Major staple across Guinea and Sudan savannas.
National staple grain in Western and Rift Valley grain belts.
Commercial maize triangle of Southern Africa.

nitrogenEffect: High nitrogen depletion. Rapidly exhausts soil N if cropped continuously.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Deep extensive rooting profile capable of extracting subsoil moisture.

description: The most widely consumed staple cereal in sub-Saharan Africa, vital for household food security and livestock feed.

rotationCompatibility.notes: Rotating with grain legumes (cowpea, soybean) contributes up to 40-60 kg/ha nitrogen equivalent.

imageSource: Wikimedia Commons (Zea mays corn cob & field)
imageAttribution: USDA Agricultural Research Service / Wikimedia Commons

name: Faba Bean

regionalSuitability.notes: Cool highland agroecology; cornerstone of cereal crop rotation.
Winter broad bean crop; staple for Ful Medames.

nitrogenEffect: Highly enriching — Fixes atmospheric nitrogen symbiosis via Rhizobium leguminosarum, leaving substantial residual N.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Stout taproot bearing profuse nodule clusters that improve soil porosity and biological health.

description: Crucial high-protein cool-season pulse in East and North Africa. Superb biological nitrogen contributor for cereal cycles.
challenges: Sensitive to terminal heat and water deficit during flowering

rotationCompatibility.notes: Ideal predecessor for bread wheat and teff; eliminates root-rot carryover.

name: Sorghum

regionalSuitability.notes: Major rainfed and mechanized clay plain grain crop.
Sudan and Sahel savannas; critical for food and beverage.
Drought-prone semi-arid lowlands and escarpments.

nitrogenEffect: Moderate depletion — Deep roots scavenge residual soil nutrients effectively.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Exceptionally deep root system with waxy cuticles and osmotic adjustment enabling survival during prolonged drought.

description: Indigenous African cereal renowned for supreme drought resilience, heat tolerance, and reliability in drylands.
advantages: Versatile food, feed, and brewing uses
challenges: Grain mold under unexpected late rains

rotationCompatibility.notes: Rotating with trap-crop cowpea triggers suicidal germination of parasitic Striga hermonthica seeds.

name: Pearl Millet

regionalSuitability.notes: The primary staple of the Sahelian sandy belt.
Central Groundnut Basin dryland cereal.
Known locally as Mahangu; foundational food security crop.

nitrogenEffect: Low depletion — Adapted to extract minimal nutrients from poor sandy soils.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Rapid early root elongation captures scarce moisture in loose sand.

description: The ultimate desert frontier grain, flourishing where temperatures exceed 40°C and rainfall drops below 300mm.
challenges: Lower commercial trade volume compared to maize

rotationCompatibility.notes: Intercropping or alternating with cowpea preserves soil fertility and breaks the cycle of Striga.

name: Cassava

regionalSuitability.notes: World's largest producer; grown extensively for garri, fufu, and industrial starch.
National dietary backbone; roots and leaves consumed.
Lake Victoria basin and coastal plains food reserve.

nitrogenEffect: Heavy potassium and phosphorus feeder; moderate nitrogen uptake over full year cycle.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Stores starch in thickened fibrous roots; dormant in drought and resumes vegetative growth upon rainfall.

description: Africa's supreme famine-security crop. Produces reliable caloric yields in degraded soils with erratic rain.
advantages: In-ground storage for months until needed
High drought tolerance via shedding leaves

rotationCompatibility.notes: Best rotated with short-season grain legumes to rebalance potassium and organic matter.

name: Rice

regionalSuitability.notes: Highest per capita consumption in Africa; terraced and lowland paddies.
Fadama irrigated floodplains and rainfed lowland valleys.
Major gravity-irrigated rice schemes in the Inner Niger Delta.

nitrogenEffect: Moderate to heavy feeder under flooded/lowland conditions.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Specialized aerenchyma tissues transport oxygen from leaves to roots in flooded soils.

description: Staple food grain undergoing exponential urban demand across Africa. Grown in upland, rainfed lowland, and irrigated systems.
challenges: Rice blast and yellow mottle virus

rotationCompatibility.notes: Dry-season legume rotation in rice paddies breaks aquatic weed cycles and replenishes soil N.

name: Common Bean

regionalSuitability.notes: Primary dietary protein source; bush and climbing bean varieties.
Ubiquitous maize intercrop (Rosecoco, Mwitemania).
Bimodal seasons allow two harvests per year.

nitrogenEffect: Positive — Fixes atmospheric nitrogen, benefiting following cereal seasons.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Moderate rooting depth with nodulation concentrated in the top 20cm of soil.

description: The quintessential grain legume of East and Central African highlands, delivering indispensable dietary protein and micronutrients.
challenges: Heat stress above 30°C causing flower drop

rotationCompatibility.notes: Classic intercropping partner with maize; fixes nitrogen while utilizing upright stalks for support.

name: Cowpea

regionalSuitability.notes: Largest global producer; grains and dry fodder are major commodities.
Grown in sandy Sahelian soils intercropped with pearl millet.
Drought-tolerant cash and subsistence pulse.

nitrogenEffect: Strongly positive — High nitrogen-fixing capacity and substantial biomass return.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Rapidly penetrating taproot accesses deep subsoil moisture in sandy soils.

description: Warm-season drought-hardy legume native to sub-Saharan Africa. Provides grains, fresh leaves, and highly valued protein-rich dry livestock fodder.

rotationCompatibility.notes: Stimulates suicidal germination of Striga hermonthica, reducing parasitic weed pressure for following cereals.

name: Groundnut

regionalSuitability.notes: The historic Senegalese Groundnut Basin.
Northern savanna commercial oil and food crop.
Key smallholder cash crop and soil enhancer.

nitrogenEffect: Positive — Fixes nitrogen and enriches light sandy soils.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Geocarpic development: flowers pollinate above ground and push pegs into the soil to mature pods.

description: Major smallholder oilseed and protein food crop, providing valuable edible oil, food paste, and nitrogen recycling.
advantages: High commercial value and oil content (45-50%)
challenges: Aflatoxin contamination (Aspergillus flavus) in dry storage
Requires loose friable soil for pegging

rotationCompatibility.notes: Preceding cereals with groundnut yields up to 20-30% boost in subsequent grain weight.

name: Soybean

regionalSuitability.notes: Commercial rotation with maize.
Southern Guinea savanna poultry feed and oil production.
Rapid commercial and smallholder expansion.

nitrogenEffect: Highly positive — Promiscuous nodulating varieties fix substantial nitrogen for subsequent crops.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Deep taproot with prominent Bradyrhizobium nodules.

description: Leading industrial legume for animal feed and oil processing, increasingly adopted by African smallholders.
advantages: Massive industrial demand from poultry industry
challenges: Pod shattering if harvest is delayed

rotationCompatibility.notes: Cornerstone of maize-soybean rotation systems across the globe and Southern Africa.

name: White Yam / Water Yam

regionalSuitability.notes: The epicenter of world yam production; deep cultural significance.
Major export commodity (Pona yam).
Savanna-forest transition zone.

nitrogenEffect: Heavy nutrient consumer requiring high organic matter.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Produces massive subterranean storage tubers on mounded or ridged seedbeds.

description: Prestigious high-value staple tuber of the West African Yam Belt. Central to cultural heritage and cuisine.
advantages: Premium market price and food preference
Good post-harvest shelf life in yam barns (4-6 months)
challenges: High seed tuber cost (takes 30% of harvest for seed)
High labor demand for mounding and staking

rotationCompatibility.notes: Traditionally planted as first crop after bush fallow; benefits from preceding legume green manures.

name: Sweet Potato

regionalSuitability.notes: One of the largest producers globally; major food security reserve.
Orange-Fleshed Sweet Potato (OFSP) biofortification leader.
Short season rotation crop on hillside terraces.

nitrogenEffect: Moderate feeder; dense foliage protects soil from erosion and conserves moisture.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Sprawling vine canopy with shallow adventitious storage tubers.

description: Fast-maturing, nutrient-dense root crop. Orange-fleshed varieties provide critical Vitamin A to rural families.
advantages: Ground-covering vines suppress weeds and halt erosion
challenges: Sweet potato weevil (Cylas spp.) during dry periods

rotationCompatibility.notes: Ideal short-cycle catch crop between major cereal seasons.

name: Cooking & Dessert Banana

regionalSuitability.notes: East African Highland Banana (Matooke) is the national staple.
Volcanic slopes and Lake Victoria basin agroforestry.
Terraced banana grooves combined with beans.

nitrogenEffect: Heavy feeder of potassium and water; perennial soil cover.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Extensive shallow root mats requiring heavy mulching to conserve moisture.

description: Perennial cornerstone staple across the Great Lakes region of East Africa, yielding food continuously year-round.
advantages: Provides microclimate and mulch for intercrops

rotationCompatibility.notes: Classic intercrop with shade coffee and climbing common beans in East African home gardens.

name: Plantain

regionalSuitability.notes: Major dietary staple and cash generator for forest farmers.
Cocoa agroforestry companion and food staple (Fufu / Ampesi).
Key ingredient in Aloco (fried plantain).

nitrogenEffect: High potassium and organic matter requirement.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Shallow rooting network requiring organic leaf litter cover.

description: Essential starch staple and companion crop across the humid tropical rainforest belt of West and Central Africa.
advantages: Excellent shade nurse crop for establishing young cocoa
High market value in urban centers
challenges: Rapid decline in yield after 3-4 ratoon cycles

rotationCompatibility.notes: Regularly interplanted into new cocoa orchards to provide crucial protective shade and interim income.

name: Cocoa

regionalSuitability.notes: World's largest cocoa producer (~40% of global supply).
Renowned for premium high-grade fermented cocoa beans.
Key forest zone export generator.

nitrogenEffect: Perennial agroforestry tree; maintains soil organic carbon via continuous leaf litter recycling.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Stout taproot reaching 1.5-2m with dense surface feeder roots under leaf mulch.

description: Global commercial cash crop producing chocolate beans. West Africa produces nearly 70% of the world's entire crop.
advantages: Maintains forest canopy in shaded agroforestry
challenges: Vulnerability to extended dry seasons under climate change
soilPreference: Acrisols (Deep, well drained, high organic matter)

rotationCompatibility.notes: Thrives under agroforestry shade trees that fix nitrogen and temper maximum temperatures.

name: Coffee (Arabica / Robusta)

regionalSuitability.notes: Birthplace and genetic reservoir of Coffea arabica; heirloom garden and forest systems.
Major Robusta native habitat and commercial export.
High-altitude specialty specialty Arabica.

nitrogenEffect: Moderate nutrient consumer; benefits substantially from nitrogen-fixing shade trees (e.g., Acacia, Erythrina).

rootCharacteristics.notes: Deep central taproot anchoring the shrub, with extensive feeder roots in the top 30cm.

description: High-value beverage cash crop indigenous to Ethiopian highlands (Arabica) and the Congo basin (Robusta).
advantages: Supports agroforestry biodiversity and carbon storage

poor: monoculture exposed to direct sun without irrigation
rotationCompatibility.notes: Intercropping Arabica coffee with highland bananas increases farmer resilience and reduces thermal stress.

imageSource: Wikimedia Commons (Coffea arabica ripe cherries on branch)

name: Barley

regionalSuitability.notes: Extremely high elevation frost-tolerant staple (food and malt barley).
Drought-prone Mediterranean cereal.
Dryland cereal for human food and animal forage.

nitrogenEffect: Moderate depletion — Tolerates saline and marginal soils better than wheat.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Dense fibrous rooting network with high salinity and drought resistance.

description: One of Africa's hardiest highland and Mediterranean cereals, flourishing at altitudes up to 3,500m in Ethiopia and in arid North African plains.
advantages: Superior cold and frost tolerance in highlands
challenges: Scald and net blotch fungal diseases
Lower grain price than wheat unless high-spec malting grade

rotationCompatibility.notes: Following faba bean significantly elevates grain plumpness and yield in Ethiopian highlands.

name: Chickpea

regionalSuitability.notes: Residual moisture crop on vertisols post-teff or post-wheat.
Winter and spring rainfed legume.

nitrogenEffect: Replenishes — fixes 40–80 kg N/ha, excellent break crop for cereals.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Deep taproot accessing residual subsoil moisture.

description: Drought-tolerant cool-season grain legume vital for highland cropping systems and biological soil restoration.
challenges: Ascochyta blight susceptibility in damp weather

rotationCompatibility.notes: Exceptional rotation partner following teff or wheat.

name: Cotton

regionalSuitability.notes: Principal commercial cash crop in the cotton basin.
Key smallholder cash crop.

nitrogenEffect: Heavy nitrogen and potassium depleter. Demands organic manure or balanced fertilization.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Extensive deep taproot system.

description: Major commercial industrial fiber and oilseed crop across Sudanian and Sahelian savanna belts.

rotationCompatibility.notes: Rotating with cowpea or groundnut suppresses bollworm soil pupae and restores nitrogen.

references: FAO Cotton Production Compendium for West Africa

name: Sugarcane

regionalSuitability.notes: Commercial rainfed and irrigated coastal/lowveld belt.
Western Kenya sugar belt.

nitrogenEffect: High biomass extraction; requires heavy nutrient replenishment or ratoon crop management.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Dense stooling root system.

description: Perennial C4 grass grown commercially for sucrose, ethanol, and biomass energy across tropical/subtropical Africa.

rotationCompatibility.notes: Break crop legumes between crop cycles replenish soil structure and organic matter.

name: Oil Palm

regionalSuitability.notes: Primary indigenous rainforest oil palm belt.
Commercial estate and smallholder belt.

nitrogenEffect: Perennial nutrient recycling via frond mulching and empty fruit bunch return.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Dense shallow radial root mat.

description: Native African perennial palm species producing the highest yield of vegetable oil per hectare worldwide.
advantages: Highest vegetable oil yield per hectare
Indigenous tree adapted to humid tropics

rotationCompatibility.notes: Intercropping legumes during first 3 immature years controls weeds and enriches nitrogen.

references: Nigerian Institute for Oil Palm Research (NIFOR)

name: Sunflower

regionalSuitability.notes: Major summer dryland oilseed crop in rotation with maize.
Central semi-arid smallholder oilseed belt.

nitrogenEffect: Moderate depleter with deep soil potassium and nitrogen scavenging capacity.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Strong taproot capable of penetrating deep subsoil layers.

description: Hardy, short-season edible oilseed crop outstanding for semi-arid zones and drought-prone summer grain belts.
advantages: Tolerates late planting when rains delay
challenges: Sclerotinia head rot in wet conditions

rotationCompatibility.notes: Outstanding rotation partner for maize, breaking corn borer cycles and utilizing subsoil moisture.

references: Agricultural Research Council - Grain Crops Institute (ARC-GCI, South Africa)

name: Sesame

regionalSuitability.notes: Vast mechanized rainfed vertisol sesame production.
Premium export white Humera sesame.

nitrogenEffect: Low to moderate nutrient extractor; leaves light residue.

rootCharacteristics.notes: Moderate taproot with fine lateral branching.

description: Extremely drought-hardy oilseed cultivated extensively in semi-arid and lowland tropical savannas of Africa.

rotationCompatibility.notes: Rotating with sorghum or cotton breaks weed and disease cycles.
